sectionBreakdown.note: A single relentless day: roughly 90-99 switchbacks climb southeast-facing, largely shadeless slopes from the Hwy 2 trailhead up through Ponderosa forest into alpine meadows near Ro…

fitnessSpec.hiking: Strong aerobic fitness required — 11 mi round trip with ~4,300 ft gain at an average grade over 18%, with steep switchbacks concentrated early in the hike
fitnessSpec.packWeight: Light day-hiking load, roughly 15-25 lb (water, layers, navigation, snow gear if early season)

partner_requirements.approachTime: Full day; 5-7 hours round trip is typical, longer if snow lingers or party is less conditioned
requiredSkills: Sustained steep trail hiking / pacing on relentless switchbacks
Basic Class 2 scrambling and route-finding along the summit ridge
Snow travel / self-arrest awareness and route-finding if climbing early season while snow lingers on upper switchbacks
Heat management — trail is exposed and reported as hot with little shade
partner_requirements.experienceLevel: Intermediate hiker comfortable with sustained steep grades and basic Class 2 off-trail/ridge scrambling near the summit; not a beginner-friendly trail due to relentless switchbacks

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Mid-July through September as the leading edge of the window; conditions remain climbable into October

July.reason: Season opens as snow melts out; lingering snow on the trail early in the month, and wildflower bloom is beginning

August.reason: Peak wildflower meadows and most reliable dry, snow-free footing on the switchbacks

October.reason: Early snow/ice possible at elevation and on the exposed switchbacks; shorter daylight window for the full 11-mile round trip

September.reason: Stable dry weather, fall colors, fewer bugs; one of the best months for the steep exposed trail

fitnessSpec.hiking: Strong multi-day hiking fitness - approach is long and remote (typically via high camp in Leroy or Phelps Creek basin), often paired with summiting Emerald Peak the same trip
fitnessSpec.packWeight: Overnight/backpacking load for the approach (camp gear, several days of food) plus a light summit pack for the scramble day

partner_requirements.approachTime: Multi-day trip typical; long approach via North Fork Entiat River Trail to a high basin camp before the summit scramble, consistent with the remote-approach note
requiredSkills: backcountry navigation (map/compass or GPS - route is not signed or consistently cairned)
self-arrest/snow travel judgment for lingering snow in the col early season
comfort with remote, low-traffic terrain (no expectation of rescue or other parties nearby)
partner_requirements.experienceLevel: Comfortable on unmaintained trail and off-trail travel with prior Class 3 scrambling experience; should be capable of basic routefinding through cairned, loose terrain without a set path

weather.typical: East-Cascades continental summer pattern - warm, dry days at elevation with cold nights; consistent with the south-aspect, high-basin setting
weather.probability: Afternoon thunderstorms are a known hazard on this route - most common July-August; plan to be off exposed ridge/summit terrain by early afternoon

seasonal_hazards.exposure: Moderate - Class 2-3 terrain with loose rock and routefinding between summits; a slip on loose sections or in the lingering col snow could result in a serious fall, compounded by the remote approach and lack of nearby help

avalanche.zone: N/A - non-glaciated summer scramble route; NWAC does not issue a forecast specific to the Entiat Mountains and this route is not climbed in avalanche season

itinerary.cal: Approach trail and high basin typically hold snow into early summer; most trip reports for this peak are from late May-June, so expect snow travel on the col and south slopes early season.

days.note: Hike the North Fork Entiat / Snow Brushy Creek Trail corridor into the basin below Emerald, Saska and Cardinal. The first miles cross old burn/blowdown before climbing steadily to a meadow camp used by most parties as their base for the col and summit push.
days.title: Backpack in to basin camp
days.objective: Reach camp near the Emerald-Saska basin (~6,800-7,200 ft)

days.note: An early, light start from camp up into the basin and onto the Emerald-Saska col, then Class 2-3 scrambling up the south slopes to the 8,404 ft summit. Most parties are back at camp by early-mid afternoon with time to rest before hiking out the next day.
days.title: Summit push via Emerald-Saska col

schedule.label: Leave camp
schedule.detail: Light day pack, cross the basin toward the col.

schedule.label: Gain the Emerald-Saska col
schedule.detail: Saddle between the two peaks; south slopes route begins here.

schedule.label: Start south slopes scramble
schedule.detail: Class 2-3 terrain, loose in spots; follow path of least resistance.

schedule.label: Summit (8,404 ft)
schedule.detail: Views across the Glacier Peak Wilderness and Chelan Mountains.

schedule.label: Begin descent
schedule.detail: Reverse the south slopes and col.

schedule.label: Back at camp
schedule.detail: Rest, refill water, prep for hike-out the next day.

days.objective: Climb Saska Peak's south slopes from the col and return to camp

days.note: Reverse the approach trail back down through the basin and along the Entiat drainage to the trailhead. A straightforward but long descent day.
days.title: Hike out
days.objective: Break camp and hike back to the trailhead

itinerary.totalNote: A 3-day backpacking trip: roughly 22 miles round trip with about 6,000 ft of gain, one full day each way for the approach/exit and a dedicated summit day via the Emerald-Saska col and Saska's south slopes.
